catalog_quote: Bambara has two level tones, low (marked by the grave accent) and high (marked by the acute accent; a circumflex is used in the phonetic transcription for the falling tone, i.e. a combination of H + L). A tonal domain most often (but not always) coincides with the word and consists of a tonally dominant syllable (the initial syllable of a domain whose tone is lexically determined) and, optionally, one or more recessive syllables (whose tones are assigned according to rules). It should be underlined that the tonally dominant character of the syllable is not equivalent with the headedness of the foot: these two phenomena are not isomorphic. ... Contrary to what was postulated in Vydrin (2014), the difference between the disyllabic feet types in Bambara can be exhaustively described in the terms of the length of the first vowel, there is no need to postulate the existence of stress. ... Th…
sweep_summary: Three stress/prosody-titled items for Bambara (bamb1269), all already in the per-language bibliography. New this search of works with stress in the title: Green 2010 (Indiana PhD, 322 pp.) was found as an open PDF on Rutgers RUcore (DOI 10.7282/T3GX49G8), saved and read; it states that no study of stress/prominence had been reported for Bamana (p.209 fn.6), that syncope is not stress-linked (p.54), that phonetic correlates of foot-head prominence are uncharacterised (p.183), and concludes Bamana is a reduced lexical tone language, not an accent language (p.257) — confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and does not supersede Vydrin 2020 (instrumental, later, same conclusion of 'featural foot and no stress'). Weidman & Rose 2006 (already held by the project) confirms: 'Bambara is not reported to have a stress system' (p.428). Green 2015 (Language 91.1, e1-e26) remains paywalled (Cambridge Core/Project MUSE; online with a university library loginonly); its abstract is silent on Bambara stress and presents uniformly trochaic L-to-R feet as segmental/tonal domains; medium priority to acquire, mainly for completeness since the dissertation it derives from has been read.archive.org).

new_statements.quote: I echo the observation in Weidman & Rose (2006) that no exploration into stress and/or prominence has previously been reported in the Bamana literature. [p.209 fn.6] ... In summary, although Colloquial Bamana has several characteristics that might lead one to suggest the eventual emergence of an accent-like prosodic system for the language, it is clear that the language (in its current state) is best analyzed as a reduced lexical tone language that utilizes word melodies and tonal feet in its conventions of tonal association. [p.257]

new_statements.reading: First-hand (fieldwork-based) monograph on Bamana prosody: no word-stress system is described or claimed; the foot (disyllabic, left-headed, parsed left-to-right) is a domain for segmental reduction and tone association, foot-head 'prominence' has no characterised phonetic correlates, vowel syncope is explicitly not stress-driven, a pitch accent reading is considered and rejected, and stress/accent is at most a possible future development. This confirms the catalog's 'tonal' (no word-stress rule) coding.

new_statements.quote: 139. Il ne semble pas exister en mandingue de tons musicaux analogues à ceux que l'on rencontre dans nombre de langues négro-africaines [...] 140. Par ailleurs, il existe en mandingue un accent tonique, un accent de durée et des accents d'intonation émotive ou logique. a) Accent tonique. 141. L'accent tonique, caractérisé en mandingue par la hauteur plus que par l'intensité, et très peu marqué en général, tombe comme en français sur la dernière syllabe du mot. 142. Si l'on a affaire à un mot composé ou dérivé, ou à un groupe de mots formant corps, il se répète sur la dernière syllabe de chacun des composants, mais se fait surtout sentir sur la dernière syllabe du dernier composant. 143. Cet accent est complètement indépendant de la durée des voyelles.
new_statements.translation: 139. There do not seem to exist in Mandingue musical tones like those found in many Negro-African languages [...] 140. On the other hand, Mandingue has a tonic accent, an accent of duration and accents of emotive or logical intonation. a) Tonic accent. 141. The tonic accent, characterised in Mandingue by pitch more than by intensity, and in general very weakly marked, falls as in French on the last syllable of the word. 142. In a compound or derived word, or a group of words forming a unit, it is repeated on the last syllable of each component, but is felt above all on the last syllable of the last component. 143. This accent is completely independent of vowel length.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog and all later work: asserts a final-syllable word accent for 'mandingue' (Malinké, Bambara, Dioula treated together) and denies lexical tone, whereas the catalog codes Bamana as tonal with no word-stress rule and Green 2010 / Creissels 1992 treat it as a tone language. Delafosse's pitch-based final 'accent' is a pre-tonological reading of the H/LH tonal patterns; the statement is historically important but superseded. Note also that the description covers Mandingue as a whole, with Bambara only one of the dialects.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-final 'accent tonique', realised mainly by pitch and weak; in compounds and derivatives it recurs on the last syllable of every component and is strongest on the final one; independent of vowel length; not marked in texts or dictionary because its placement is 'soumis à une régularité absolue' (§146). Separate lexically unpredictable 'accent de durée' (length), which in disyllabic roots never falls on the second syllable except in loans (§150). Lexical tone is explicitly denied (§139).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §142: in compounds the accent is repeated on the final syllable of each component, strongest on the last (a weaker accent on non-final components)
new_statements.exceptions: §146 claims no exceptions (absolutely regular placement); §150 length accent exceptions in loanwords (wala, dyamaa, kaso)
new_statements.identity_note: Dumestre & Hosaka 2000 describes the Kolona dialect (southern Mali), not standard (Bamako) Bambara, and reports its tone assignment as identical to the standard. Delafosse 1929 describes 'mandingue' as a single language with Malinké, Bambara and Dioula as dialects; Bambara is not separated in the accent section. Masiuk 1987-88 refers to Bamako Bambara. Creissels 1992 covers standard Bambara and the Ségou variety.

new_statements.quote: Compte tenu de la confusion qui règne actuellement dans l'emploi des termes de 'ton' et d''accent', il importe de poser comme point de départ que le bambara est indéniablement une langue à tons si on entend par là une langue dans laquelle une différence de hauteur ou de contour mélodique localisée sur une syllabe, le contexte phonétique et la structure morphosyntaxique restant identiques, peut constituer la seule trace d'une commutation entre deux unités significatives [p. 8-9] ... on ne connaît pas de langue à accent [...] où la syllabe accentuée se reconnaîtrait systématiquement par une hauteur mélodique inférieure à celle des autres syllabes. Or le bambara oblige à abandonner cette hypothèse [p. 27]
new_statements.translation: Given the confusion that currently reigns in the use of the terms 'tone' and 'accent', it is important to state as a starting point that Bambara is undeniably a tone language, if by that one means a language in which a difference of pitch or melodic contour located on one syllable, with phonetic context and morphosyntactic structure held constant, can be the only trace of a commutation between two meaningful units [pp. 8-9] ... no accent language is known in which the accented syllable would be systematically recognised by a pitch lower than that of the other syllables. Yet Bambara forces us to abandon this hypothesis [p. 27]
new_statements.citation: Creissels, Denis (1992). Tonologie du bambara: Bilan et perspectives. Mandenkan 24. pp. 1–45.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bambara is a tone language with a binary H/L opposition (minimal pairs, never more than two levels on a syllable). No word stress is described. The author explicitly rejects reading the restricted tone system as an accent system: the marked tone is Low, and no accent language marks its accented syllable by lower pitch; he concedes only (pp. 42-43) that the marked tone's rightward shift 'evoke[s]' accent-like behaviour, 'sans pour autant tomber dans la confusion dénoncée ci-dessus entre ton et accent'.

new_statements.quote: [p.265, abstract] It seems unnecessary to postulate stress in Bambara. [p.266] These foot types depart from traditional analyses of prosodic feet that appeal to ideas of trochaicity vs. iambicity, but I will argue that such an approach arrives at stronger generalizations about the language, given that phenomena related to headedness, such as stress, have no clear correlates in Bambara. [p.294] The crucial question is: do we really need to postulate headedness for a featural foot in a stressless language? ... One could suggest an alternative solution, namely to postulate two types of feet, heavy (with a long V1) and light (with a short V1), without postulating syllable headedness.
new_statements.citation: Vydrin, Valentin. 2020. Featural foot in Bambara. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 41(2): 265-300.
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata: 36 pp., title 'Journal of African Languages and Linguistics', Distiller Jan 2021) and its extracted text. Header line 1 reads 'JALL 2020; 41(2): 265-300', 'Valentin Vydrin / Featural foot in Bambara', DOI 10.1515/jall-2020-2012 = the cited work. All three quoted pieces are present verbatim at the stated locators: (a) abstract p.265 'It seems unnecessary to postulate stress in Bambara.'; (b) Introduction p.266 'These foot types depart from traditional analyses of prosodic feet that appeal to ideas of trochaicity vs. iambicity, but I will argue that such an approach arrives at stronger generalizations about the language, given that phenomena related to headedness, such as…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Bamana coded tonal, empty stress rule) and as the existing statement from Green 2010 (no word-stress system; foot is a domain for reduction and tone, not stress). Vydrin goes further than Green in denying even foot headedness, and disputes Green's trochaic parsing and Leben/Weidman & Rose's 'tonal foot', but none of these disagreements concern the presence or placement of word stress: all treat Bambara as stressless.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bambara is treated as a stressless tone language: the (featural) foot is a mono- or disyllabic rhythmic unit parsed by morphology and segmental phonotactics (left-to-right directionality secondary), relevant to vowel length/elision and partly to tone realization, but with no syllable headedness and no stress; disyllabic feet are 'heavy' (long V1) or 'light' (short, reducible V1, V2 long by default), an opposition that is length-based, not stress-based. The tonal domain is the prosodic word, not the foot.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none; the author explicitly declines to posit any head/prominence within the foot. He notes phonetically (p.293) that in a light foot V1 'is usually pronounced louder than the second' while V2 is longer, so the light foot is 'underspecified with respect to syllable prominence' and may surface iambic-like (usual in Standard Bambara) or trochaic-like.
new_statements.exceptions: Identity/variety: the analysis is for Standard Bambara (Bamako-based); Vydrin says Green's (2010, 2015) trochaic-foot analysis rests on 'Colloquial Bambara', where vowel-length contrasts seem lost, and 'may be correct for that variety' but should not be extended to Standard Bambara (p.292-293). He also records (§6.4, p.296) that his own earlier work (Vydrin 2008a, 2010) called the second syllable of the disyllabic foot stressed (iambic), and Vydrin 2014 posited iambic/trochaic/neutral feet with stressed syllables, positions he now abandons in favour of two stressless foot types.
new_statements.identity_note: Vydrin describes Standard Bambara (Bamako-based standard variety, with phonemic vowel length in foot-initial position); he notes Green's data come from 'Colloquial Bambara', a variety in which length contrasts appear to have been lost, and limits Green's trochaic analysis to that variety at most.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement: Delafosse 1929 (§§139-146, pp. 104-105) asserts that 'mandingue' (Malinké, Bambara, Dioula) has no musical tones and instead a weak, pitch-based 'accent tonique' on the final syllable of every word (repeated on each component of compounds, strongest on the last). Every later source opened here treats Bambara as a tone language: Creissels 1992 states it is 'indéniablement une langue à tons' and argues against an accentual reinterpretation, and Dumestre 1981, Dumestre & Hosaka 2000, Vydrine 1991/1999 describe lexical H vs. L/rising tone patterns without any stress. Delafosse's final 'accent' is a pre-tonological perception of the H/LH tonal patterns and is superseded; it should not change the catalog's classification. No other conflicts.

sources.citation: Dumestre, Gerard (1984). Contribution à l'étude des tons du bambara. Mandenkan 7. pp. 63–74.
sources.note: No statement on word stress; the language is treated as a two-tone language throughout, which is compatible with the catalog's tonal coding and with Green 2010's 'no stress system' finding. The intensity remark is about the phonetic realisation of tonal raising before L (a phrase-level sandhi effect on the final segment, also cued by pitch or pause), so it does not amount to a stress rule and does not contradict Green. The notes (p. 74) cite Creissels 1982 'Ton et accent en mandinka' (Leiden colloquium, unpublished), which concerns Mandinka, not Bamana. Read all twelve journal pages (63-74).

sources.quote: Tonal African languages are particularly problematic, as correlates of stress or metrical prominence are often not well defined or are absent altogether. ... An exception to this is Bambara, where research implicates a pivotal role for foot structure in segmental and tonal processes. ... The data presented support a claim that all Bambara feet are uniformly trochaic and parsed from left to right in all instances. I intend to illustrate that Bambara segmental and tonal feet are a single, structurally unified prosodic entity.
sources.note: The competing metrical analysis (all feet trochaic, parsed L-to-R, segmental and tonal feet unified); record's tone_note summarises it second-hand via Vydrin 2020. Needed to confirm Green treats foot heads as domains for syncope/tone rather than word stress (abstract read on Cambridge Core supports this).
